tool.name: MultiSunHillshade
tool.summary: Computes a hillshade as the weighted average of standard hillshades from two to eight sun positions, each with its own azimuth, inclination, and weight - the classic Swiss multiple-light-source strategy. Optional per-sun cast shadows (dimmed before averaging) and hypsometric shading (applied once, after). Correct on geographic (latitude/longitude) rasters.
tool.usage:
A single-source hillshade emphasizes terrain that happens to be lit obliquely but washes out slopes that face directly toward or away from the light. Blending hillshades from several sun positions - the classic Swiss multiple-light-source relief-shading strategy - keeps detail visible in every orientation. This tool computes a standard hillshade for each of two to eight sun positions, each with its own azimuth, inclination, and weight, and averages them into a single raster using the weights (which total 100 percent).
Choose the number of sun positions first: the dialog then shows an azimuth, inclination, and weight box for each sun. Weights are pre-filled with a balanced split: with N suns, the first N - 1 weights are 100/N rounded to the nearest integer, and the last is 100 minus the others (two suns get 50 and 50; three get 33, 33, and 34). The last sun's weight is always calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited; because it is not an input box, it is displayed in the read-only Automatically calculated weight line, which updates as you change the other weights to keep the total at 100. The first two suns are pre-filled from a pleasing two-sun combination (280/35 and 350/45); later suns step 45 degrees clockwise at a 45-degree inclination. All positions are fully editable, and your last-used choices are remembered with the project.
Optional cast shadows are computed separately for each sun (each sun position casts its own shadows), and each sun's shadowed cells are dimmed to the shadow-brightness percentage before the averaging - so ground shadowed from one sun but lit by another stays partly lit, a naturally soft penumbra effect. Optional hypsometric shading (darkening low elevations) is applied once, to the final averaged hillshade.
Unlike the standard hillshade, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: the horizontal and vertical dimensions of each cell are recomputed for every row of the raster from the spheroid, so slopes and shading are correct at any latitude without projecting the DEM first. Projected DEMs use faster constant-cell planar formulas. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet.
This tool is one part of the classic "Swiss style" of relief presentation (after Eduard Imhof and the Swiss cartographers, whose hand-drawn conventions Kurt Brassel first automated), which combines three strategies: illuminating the terrain from multiple directions, elevation-based tone adjustments that mimic atmospheric perspective, and softening of the final image. In this toolbox the MDOW Hillshade and Multi-Sun Hillshade tools provide the multi-directional illumination, the hypsometric-shading options and the Simple Hypsometric Shading tool provide the elevation-based tinting, and the Blurred Hillshade tool provides the softening.
Environments. By default the output matches the input grid exactly (same extent, cell size, and coordinate system). Honored environments: Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System, all applied as finishing steps to the computed hillshade - the extent clips it (with the snap raster aligning the clip window), the cell size resamples it, and the output coordinate system reprojects it. Because the shading is always computed first from the full-resolution source DEM, cells at a clipped edge carry true hillshade values, and resampling or reprojecting smooths the finished shading rather than recomputing it on the new grid. The Mask environment is not honored, and pyramids are always built with bilinear resampling regardless of the Pyramid environment. The output carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step.
Symbolize the result with ArcGIS Pro's standard stretch renderers.
Reference: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the hillshade from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.
The output multi-sun hillshade raster (integer, 0 to the number of hillshade levels; NoData where the DEM has NoData or at the outer edge). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.
How many sun positions to blend, 2 to 8. The dialog shows an azimuth, inclination, and weight box for each; choosing a new count re-fills the weights with a balanced split.
The compass direction of sun 1, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north.
The angle of sun 1 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees.
The relative weight of sun 1 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited.
The compass direction of sun 2, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north.
The angle of sun 2 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees.
The relative weight of sun 2 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited.
The compass direction of sun 3, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 3.
The angle of sun 3 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 3.

The relative weight of sun 3 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 3.
The compass direction of sun 4, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 4.
The angle of sun 4 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 4.

The relative weight of sun 4 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 4.
The compass direction of sun 5, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 5.
The angle of sun 5 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 5.

The relative weight of sun 5 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 5.
The compass direction of sun 6, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 6.
The angle of sun 6 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 6.

The relative weight of sun 6 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 6.
The compass direction of sun 7, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 7.
The angle of sun 7 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 7.

The relative weight of sun 7 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 7.
The compass direction of sun 8, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 8.
The angle of sun 8 above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 8.

The relative weight of sun 8 in the average, 0 to 100 percent. The last visible weight is calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights and cannot be edited. Shown when the number of sun positions is at least 8.

A read-only line showing the last sun's weight, which is always calculated automatically as 100 minus the other weights (for example, "Sun 3: weight (percent) automatically calculated as 34"). It updates as you change the other weights; anything typed here is ignored.

The number of gray levels in the output: values run from 0 (fully shaded) to this number (fully lit). Use 255 to match the standard Esri hillshade, or a small number for a posterized cartographic look. A larger number gives a higher-precision hillshade, although the added precision may not be visually apparent on a computer screen.
Darkens the hillshade at lower elevations to add an impression of overall relief. Applied once, to the final averaged hillshade. The amount is set by the Hypsometric strength.

How strongly low elevations are darkened, 0 to 100 percent. At strength s, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum. The default is 50.
Multiplies the elevations before shading, exaggerating (greater than 1) or flattening (less than 1) the relief. The default is 1 (no exaggeration).

param.name: model_shadows
param.displayname: Model cast shadows (per sun, before averaging)

dialogReference.para: Computes cast shadows separately for each sun position and dims each sun's shadowed cells to the shadow brightness before the hillshades are averaged - ground hidden from one sun but lit by another stays partly lit. Computed with a fast single-pass sweep per sun; requires enough memory to hold the whole DEM at once.

The percentage of its unshadowed value that a shadowed cell keeps in each individual sun's hillshade, 0 to 100. The same value applies to every sun. Use 0 for fully black per-sun shadows or larger values to keep relief detail visible inside them. The default is 20.

scriptExample.title: Multi-Sun Hillshade example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Blend three sun positions with custom weights and per-sun cast shadows.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.MultiSunHillshade( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_MultiSun", elev_units="Meters", n_suns=3, azimuth_1=280, altitude_1=35, weight_1=40, azimuth_2=350, altitude_2=45, weight_2=40, azimuth_3=135, altitude_3=60, weight_3=20, levels=255, model_shadows=True, shadow_dim=20)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Weighted average of standard hillshades from multiple sun positions (Swiss multiple-light-source strategy), with per-sun cast shadows, hypsometric shading, and correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Multi-sun hillshade raster: a weighted average of standard hillshades computed from two to eight sun positions, each with its own azimuth, inclination, and weight (weights total 100 percent; the dialog pre-fills a balanced split and calculates the last weight automatically). Blending several light sources brings out terrain features that a single sun washes out. Optional cast shadows are computed per sun and dimmed to a chosen brightness before the averaging; optional hypsometric shading darkens low elevations, applied once to the averaged result. Cell dimensions on geographic DEMs are recomputed for every row from the spheroid, so shading is accurate at any latitude without projecting first. The output matches the input grid (honoring the Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System environments as post-computation finishing steps) and carries statistics and a histogram.
